readings.title: Our neighbourhood: the Solar System
readings.text:
The Earth is not alone in space. It is part of the Solar System, which has a star in the middle: the Sun. Eight planets travel around the Sun. The closest is Mercury and the furthest is Neptune.

Every planet is very different. Jupiter is the biggest of all: more than a thousand Earths could fit inside it. Mars looks reddish because its ground has a lot of rust in it. And the Earth is the only planet where we know there is life.

readings.title: Instruments of the orchestra
readings.text:
In an orchestra, many musicians play at the same time, and each one has an instrument. The instruments are put into families.

The string family has violins, violas, cellos and double basses: they make a sound when you move a bow across the strings. The woodwind and brass families include flutes, clarinets and trumpets: you blow into them. Percussion, like drums and cymbals, makes a sound when you hit it. In front of everyone is the conductor, who keeps the beat with a small stick called a baton.

readings.title: The Paralympic Games
readings.text:
Every four years, after the Olympic Games, the Paralympic Games take place. Athletes with a physical, visual or intellectual disability compete in them.

The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960. The idea started in a hospital in England, where a doctor called Ludwig Guttmann used sport to help soldiers who had been injured in the war to get better.

Today there are sports like wheelchair basketball, swimming and goalball, a game for blind and partially sighted players in which the ball has bells inside. Paralympic athletes show that talent and hard work have no limits.

readings.title: The cell: the unit of life
readings.text:
All living things, from a tiny bacterium to a huge whale, are made of cells. A cell is the smallest part of a living thing that can carry out the life processes on its own: nutrition, interaction and reproduction.

Some living things have only one cell. They are called unicellular, like bacteria. Others, like plants and animals, have millions of cells. They are called multicellular.

Most cells have three main parts. The membrane is a thin layer around the cell. It lets some substances in and keeps others out. The cytoplasm is the inside of the cell, a thick liquid with small parts called organelles. The genetic material has the instructions for the cell to work and to divide.

Animal cells and plant cells are similar, but plant cells also have a hard cell wall and chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are green organelles where the plant makes its food using sunlight.

The smallest part of a living thing that can carry out the life processes
questions.explanation: It is “the smallest part of a living thing that can carry out the life processes on its own”.

readings.title: The Neolithic: learning to farm
readings.text:
For thousands of years, people lived by hunting, fishing and gathering fruit. They were nomads: they moved from place to place, following animals and looking for food. This period is called the Palaeolithic.

About 10,000 years ago, in the Middle East, some groups discovered that they could plant seeds and harvest crops. They also started to domesticate animals like goats, sheep and cattle. The Neolithic had begun.

Farming changed everything. People did not need to move to find food, so many of them settled in one place and built the first villages, with houses of mud and stone. Sometimes they produced more food than they needed, and they could store this surplus or exchange it.

Over time, new jobs appeared, like the potter, who made clay pots to store grain, and the weaver. That is why many historians talk about the “Neolithic Revolution”.

readings.title: The Earth’s climates
readings.text:
Weather is what the atmosphere is like at one moment: today it is raining, tomorrow it will be sunny. Climate is the usual weather in a place over many years.

The two most important parts of climate are temperature and precipitation, that is, the rain or snow that falls. They depend mostly on latitude, the distance from a place to the equator. Near the equator, the sun’s rays hit the Earth directly, so it is hot all year. Near the poles, the rays arrive at an angle, so it is very cold.

That is why the Earth has large climate zones. In the hot zone, around the equator, there are equatorial, tropical and desert climates. In the two temperate zones, summers and winters are different. The Mediterranean climate of Valencia is in a temperate zone. In the two cold zones, near the poles, winters are very long and summers are short and cool.

Other things also matter, like altitude and the sea: it is colder in the mountains, and temperatures are milder on the coast.

readings.title: How the brain learns
readings.text: Every time you learn something new, tiny cells in your brain called neurons form new connections with each other. The more you practise, the stronger these connections become, rather like a path through a field that gets clearer each time someone walks along it. This is why practising a little every day is more effective than doing a lot once a week. Sleep also plays an important role: while you rest, your brain sorts and strengthens what you learned during the day. So making mistakes, practising and sleeping well are all part of learning.

Nobody knows exactly why it was built, but on the longest day of the year the Sun rises in line with the stones, which suggests that the builders studied the sky carefully. Today, thousands of people visit it to watch the summer sunrise.

'Pyjamas' and 'shampoo' came from India, 'chocolate' and 'tomato' from the Aztec language Nahuatl through Spanish, and 'kindergarten' from German. The Vikings gave us 'sky' and 'egg', while the Normans brought thousands of French words, such as 'beef' and 'castle'. Every time you speak English, you are using words that have crossed oceans and centuries to reach you.

readings.title: A house in space
readings.text:

The station moves so fast that it goes all the way around the Earth in about ninety minutes. That is why astronauts see about sixteen sunrises every day. readings.title: Sorolla, the painter of light
readings.text:
Joaquín Sorolla was born in Valencia, in Spain, in 1863. He loved drawing from a young age, and he became one of the most famous Spanish painters of his time.

People call Sorolla “the painter of light”. He liked painting outdoors, especially on the beaches of Valencia: children swimming, fishermen, boats and white sails blowing in the wind. He painted quickly, with loose brushstrokes, to catch the sunlight before it changed.

Today you can see many of his paintings at the Sorolla Museum in Madrid, which used to be his home. When you look at them, you can almost hear the sea and feel the summer heat.

readings.title: Solids, liquids and gases
readings.text:
Everything around us is matter: water, air, a table and even our own bodies. Matter is made of tiny particles that we cannot see. The way these particles move and join together explains the three main states of matter.

In solids, the particles are very close together and hardly move; they only vibrate. That is why solids have a fixed shape and volume. In liquids, the particles are close together but can slide past each other, so liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. In gases, the particles are far apart and move very fast in all directions, so gases fill all the space they can.

A substance can change from one state to another when its temperature changes. When we heat ice, its particles move more and more until the solid becomes a liquid. This is melting. If we keep heating, the water boils and turns into steam. This is evaporation. When it cools down, the opposite happens: steam condenses into drops, and liquid water freezes into ice.

Each substance changes state at a particular temperature. Pure water, for example, melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level.

questions.explanation: “The particles are very close together and hardly move.”

readings.title: Lords and peasants in the Middle Ages
readings.text:
In Europe, for a large part of the Middle Ages, society was organised in a system called feudalism. After the fall of the Roman Empire, kings were weak and there were many wars and invasions. To stay safe, many peasants asked powerful nobles, called lords, to protect them.

A lord owned an area of land called a fief. He received it from the king in exchange for loyalty and military help. On the fief there was the lord’s castle, the fields and the peasants’ villages. The peasants worked the land. In exchange for protection, they gave the lord part of their harvest, paid taxes and worked on his land for free on some days.

Feudal society had three groups, called estates. The nobles fought in wars. The clergy, made up of bishops, priests and monks, prayed. The peasants, who were the great majority, worked to feed everyone. People were born into an estate, and it was very difficult to change.

From the 11th century, towns and trade grew, and a new group appeared: the bourgeoisie. They were merchants and craftspeople who did not depend on any lord.

options: Kings were weak and there were wars and invasions
questions.explanation: “Kings were weak and there were many wars and invasions.”

readings.title: How many of us are there?
readings.text:
In 1800, about one billion people lived on Earth. Today there are more than eight billion. Demography is the science that studies how population changes, and it uses some basic data.

The birth rate is the number of births in a year, and the death rate is the number of deaths. If more people are born than die, the population grows. This is called natural increase. Migration also matters: people who arrive in a country are immigrants, and people who leave are emigrants.

Population is not spread out evenly. Some areas, like southern and eastern Asia, western Europe and many coasts, have a lot of people because they have a mild climate, good land or a lot of jobs. Other areas, like deserts, high mountains and polar regions, are almost empty because it is very hard to live there.

Each country is also different. In many African countries, the population is young because many babies are born. In Spain, few babies are born and people live a long time, so the population is ageing: there are more and more older people and fewer young people.

readings.title: Saturday at the food bank
readings.text:
Every Saturday morning, Ellie, who is fifteen, volunteers at the food bank in her town in the north of England. She sorts tins and packets, checks the dates and helps to pack bags for families who need them.

At first she was nervous. She didn't know anybody, and she was worried about making mistakes. But the other volunteers were friendly, and after a few weeks she felt part of the team. Now she even shows new volunteers what to do.

'The best part is when a family says thank you,' she says. 'You realise that a small thing, like two hours on a Saturday, can really help someone.'

Ellie has also learnt a lot. She is better at organising things, she is more confident when she talks to adults, and she has made new friends of all ages. Next year she wants to start a collection point at her school.

readings.title: The map that changed travel
readings.text:
In the early 1930s, the map of the London Underground was a mess. It showed the exact position of every station, so the lines in the city centre were squeezed together and the stations far away were spread out. Passengers found it very hard to read.

Harry Beck, an engineer who drew electrical circuits, had an idea. Passengers underground, he thought, don't need to know exact distances. They only need to know the order of the stations and where to change lines. So he drew the lines straight, only at 90 or 45 degrees, and put the same space between all the stations.

At first, the managers thought the design was too strange. But when it was printed in 1933, passengers loved it. Today, cities all over the world use maps that follow Beck's idea.

Beck's story shows that sometimes the best solution is not to show more information, but to show the right information.

readings.title: Sleep is training too
readings.text:
Many top athletes have something in common that you cannot see in competitions: they take sleep very seriously. They know that while we sleep, the body repairs our muscles, gets our energy back and stores what we have learnt during the day, whether it is a new skill or a maths lesson.

Experts recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night. However, many of them do not. One reason is screens: the light from a phone at night tricks the brain, which delays the feeling of sleepiness, and messages and videos keep us awake for “just five more minutes”.

Not getting enough sleep has consequences. It is harder to concentrate, we get annoyed more easily, we perform worse at sport and the risk of injury goes up.

A few simple tips can help: go to bed and get up at the same time, leave your phone outside the bedroom and avoid hard exercise just before bed. Sleeping well is not a waste of time: it is part of your training.

readings.title: Do machines think?
readings.text:
Today we talk to voice assistants, get video recommendations and translate texts in seconds thanks to artificial intelligence (AI). Some programs can write essays or create pictures from a single sentence. With such surprising results, it is easy to wonder whether these machines think like us.

Most experts give a more careful answer. These systems learn by analysing huge amounts of data and finding patterns: which word usually comes after another, or what a cat looks like in thousands of photos. That is why their answers can sound very convincing. However, they do not have experiences or understand the world the way people do. And sometimes they are completely wrong while sounding completely sure.

That is why we should use them critically. An AI can help us organise ideas or revise, but if we let it do all the work, we do not learn. We also need to check the information it gives us, just as we would with any website.

AI is a powerful tool. Whether it makes us better or lazier depends largely on how we choose to use it.

readings.title: The journey of food
readings.text:
When you eat a sandwich, a long journey begins. The digestive system breaks food down into very small substances called nutrients. The body can absorb them and use them to get energy, to grow and to repair itself.

It all starts in the mouth. Your teeth crush the food, and saliva makes it wet and starts to break down some nutrients, like the starch in bread. This forms a ball of food that you swallow. It travels down the oesophagus, pushed by the movement of its muscles.

In the stomach, the food is mixed for a few hours with very acidic gastric juices and becomes a kind of thick liquid called chyme. Then it moves into the small intestine, a tube about seven metres long, folded up inside the abdomen. There, juices from the liver and the pancreas finish digestion. The walls of the small intestine are covered in tiny folds called villi, and nutrients pass through them into the blood.

Whatever cannot be used goes to the large intestine, where most of the water is absorbed. The waste forms faeces, which leave the body through the anus. That is why it is important to drink water and eat fibre, which helps this last part work well.

readings.title: Inside the atom
readings.text:
About 2,400 years ago, the Greek philosopher Democritus had an idea: if you cut something in half again and again, in the end you get a piece that cannot be divided. He called it an atom, which means “uncuttable” in Greek. For centuries it was only an idea, but today we know that all matter is made of atoms, and that atoms do have parts.

In the centre of the atom is the nucleus. It is very small, but it has almost all the mass. It contains protons, which have a positive electric charge, and neutrons, which have no charge. Electrons move around the nucleus. They are much lighter and have a negative charge. An atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so overall it is neutral.

What makes one chemical element different from another is the number of protons, called the atomic number. Every hydrogen atom has one proton, every carbon atom has six and every oxygen atom has eight.

In the 19th century, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev put the known elements in a table according to their properties. He left gaps for elements that had not been discovered yet and predicted what they would be like. When they were found, his predictions were right. His idea is the basis of the periodic table we use today, with more than a hundred elements.

readings.title: What do people work in?
readings.text:
Economic activities are the things people do to produce goods and provide services. To study them, we put them into three sectors.

The primary sector gets resources directly from nature: farming, fishing and forestry. The oranges of Valencia and the rice from the Albufera are products of the primary sector.

The secondary sector turns those raw materials into manufactured products. It includes industry, construction and energy production. A factory that turns clay into tiles, like the ones in Castellón, or a car factory belongs to this sector.

The tertiary sector does not make objects. It provides services for people: shops, transport, education, healthcare, tourism and banking. A teacher, a doctor and a shop assistant all work in the tertiary sector.

The importance of each sector has changed over time. A hundred years ago, most people in Spain worked on the land. With industrialisation, the secondary sector grew, and today about three out of four workers are in services. That is why we say we live in a service economy.

readings.title: Is a gap year worth it?
readings.text:
In the UK, some students take a 'gap year' between finishing school and starting university. They might work, travel or volunteer abroad. But is it a good idea?

Supporters say that a gap year helps young people to become more independent and to discover what they really want to study. Students who have worked for a year often appreciate the value of money and arrive at university more motivated.

On the other hand, critics point out that a gap year can be expensive, especially if it involves travelling. Some students also find it difficult to return to studying after a long break, and a few never go back at all.

In my view, a gap year is worth it only if it is planned. A year spent learning a skill, saving money or helping others can be one of the most valuable experiences of your life. A year spent doing nothing, however, is simply a year lost.

readings.title: Alan Turing and the code breakers
readings.text:
During the Second World War, the German army sent secret messages using a machine called Enigma. The messages were in code, and the settings of the machine changed every day, so breaking the code seemed impossible.

At Bletchley Park, a country house north of London, thousands of people worked in secret to read those messages. One of them was Alan Turing, a brilliant mathematician. Together with other code breakers, he designed a machine called the Bombe, which helped to discover the Enigma settings much faster than people could by hand.

Historians believe that the work done at Bletchley Park shortened the war and saved many lives. However, it was kept secret for decades, so the people who did it received little recognition at the time.

Turing is also remembered as one of the fathers of computer science. His ideas about machines that can follow instructions — and even 'think' — are still discussed today. Since 2021, his face has appeared on the Bank of England's £50 note.

readings.title: Was there water on Mars?
readings.text:
Seen from Earth, Mars is a reddish dot in the sky. Close up, it is a cold, dusty desert, with an atmosphere so thin that we could not breathe in it. And yet scientists are convinced that billions of years ago, rivers flowed across its surface and there were lakes.

How do they know? Photos taken by satellites show dry river beds, deltas and rocks that only form when there is water. Also, there are ice caps at the poles of Mars, and more ice has been found under the ground.

Liquid water cannot stay on the surface for long today: the air pressure is so low that it would quickly turn into gas or freeze. That is why robot explorers look for clues from the past. The Perseverance rover landed in 2021 in Jezero Crater, where there was once a lake, to collect rock samples that could be brought back to Earth in the future.

The big question is still open: if Mars had water, did it ever have life? Finding the answer could change what we know about our place in the universe.

readings.title: Guernica: a painted scream
readings.text:
On 26 April 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian planes supporting General Franco’s forces bombed the Basque town of Gernika. It was market day. Much of the town was destroyed and many civilians were killed; historians still discuss the exact number.

At the time, Pablo Picasso was living in Paris. He had been asked to paint a mural for the Spanish Republic’s pavilion at that year’s International Exhibition. Shocked by the news, he decided that his work would show the horror of the bombing. In just over a month, he painted a canvas almost eight metres wide.

Guernica does not show planes or explosions. Instead, there are twisted figures: a mother screaming with her dead child in her arms, an injured horse, a bull and a light bulb that looks like an eye. Picasso used only black, white and grey, like the photos in the newspapers.

Picasso did not want the painting to go to Spain until democracy returned. It finally arrived in 1981. Today it hangs in the Reina Sofía Museum in Madrid and has become a symbol against war all over the world.

readings.title: The Industrial Revolution
readings.text:
In the late 18th century, a change began in Great Britain that was so deep it is called the Industrial Revolution. In just a few decades it changed the way people produced goods, worked and lived, first in Europe and then in much of the world.

The key change was mechanisation: work that had been done by hand or with animals began to be done by machines. The most important invention was the steam engine, improved by James Watt in the second half of the 18th century. It burned coal to produce movement. It was first used in the textile industry, where new machines made cloth much faster and more cheaply than craftspeople could.

The steam engine also changed transport. Railways and steamships carried raw materials and products to distant places quickly, and trade grew.

Factories were built in towns and cities, and thousands of people from the countryside moved there to find work. This created a new social class: the working class. Their conditions were very hard: working days of up to fourteen hours, low wages, child labour and unhealthy neighbourhoods. To defend their rights, workers joined together in trade unions, and little by little they won improvements such as shorter working hours.

Meanwhile, the owners of factories and banks became rich and gained political power. Society stopped being divided by birth and started to be divided by wealth: it became a class society.

readings.title: DNA: the instruction book
readings.text:
Why do you have your mother’s eye colour or curly hair like your grandfather? The answer is DNA, a molecule found in the nucleus of almost all your cells. It contains the information needed to build a living thing and make it work.

DNA has the shape of a double helix, like a spiral staircase. Its structure was described in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick, thanks largely to X-ray images taken by the scientist Rosalind Franklin. The steps of the staircase are made of four bases, shown by the letters A, T, C and G. Their order works like a code: just as letters make words, bases make instructions.

A piece of DNA with the instructions for one particular feature is called a gene. Humans have about twenty thousand genes, arranged in 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs. In each pair, one chromosome comes from the mother and the other from the father. That is why we look like both of them but are not identical to either.

In the mid-19th century, long before anyone knew about DNA, a monk called Gregor Mendel had already discovered, by crossing pea plants, that some features are dominant and others are recessive: a recessive feature can disappear in one generation and come back in the next. Today, genetics helps doctors diagnose diseases, helps farmers improve crops and even helps the police solve crimes.

readings.title: The laws of motion
readings.text:
A force is any push or pull that can change how an object moves or change its shape. Pushing a trolley, kicking a ball and stretching an elastic band are all forces. Forces are measured in newtons (N), named after the English scientist Isaac Newton, who in 1687 published three laws that explain how objects move.

The first law, or law of inertia, says that an object stays still, or keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless a force acts on it. That is why, when a bus stops suddenly, the passengers lurch forward: their bodies tend to keep moving.

The second law links force and acceleration, which is a change in speed. The bigger the force, the bigger the acceleration; and the more mass an object has, the more force you need to accelerate it. It is summed up in the formula F = m × a. That is why it is easier to push an empty shopping trolley than a full one.

The third law, or law of action and reaction, says that when one object pushes on another, the second object pushes back with a force that is equal and opposite. When we swim, we push the water backwards and the water pushes us forwards. Rockets work in the same way: they push gases down, and the gases push them up.
